evidence.quote: The byway starts at an intersection with SR-24 and immediately turns north-northeast through mountainous terrain before descending into a basin where Fish Lake is located. evidence.claim: Utah designated the route a state scenic byway in 1990; the Utah Office of Tourism highlights its mountain scenery, high sagebrush flats and alpine lake.
evidence.quote: Designated April 9, 1990, on SR-25 between SR-24 and Johnson Valley Reservoir.

evidence.claim: the Utah Office of Tourism highlights its mountain scenery, high sagebrush flats and alpine lake.
evidence.quote: This road trip through lush mountain scenery and high sagebrush flats is highlighted by a visit to a very pretty alpine lake.

evidence.claim: The 29.6-mile corridor includes SR-25 and county roads, continuing beyond the numbered state highway through Fishlake National Forest.
evidence.quote: Fishlake Scenic Byway is a route of 29.6 mi (47.6 km) that traverses mainly through the Fishlake National Forest, Utah. The byway comprises SR-25 and County Roads FAS-2554 and FAS-3268

evidence.claim: The lake road entered the state highway system in 1918 and received the number SR-25 in 1927.
evidence.quote: The road from SR-24 at Plateau Junction east to Fish Lake was added to the state highway system in 1918, and numbered SR-25 by the state legislature in 1927.

evidence.claim: A federal aid project moved its western end south to Fish Lake Junction in 1935.

evidence.claim: The scenic designation later reached beyond the lake: in November 1992, the byway extended along Fremont River Road from Johnson Valley Reservoir to SR-72.

evidence.claim: Start at Highway 24 and climb into Fishlake National Forest, four miles along Highway 25.

evidence.claim: After crossing the Fremont River at Zedds Meadow, the road climbs steeply, then descends through drier country toward Highway 72.
evidence.quote: Highway 25 crosses the Fremont River at Zedds Meadow. The road rises quickly and steeply for about 1 mile, then begins a long descent into the valley on the other side. The landscape is drier on the far side, with fewer trees and more open views.

evidence.claim: Near the lower river crossing, Mill Meadow Dam holds a small reservoir; Highway 72 lies three miles farther along.
evidence.quote: The road crosses the Fremont River again, where the now greatly expanded stream announces the small earthwork dam, Mill Meadow Dam, just downstream. There are lovely spots to camp along the little reservoir here. It is 3 miles farther to the intersection with Highway 72

evidence.claim: Pando’s estimated 47,000 aspen stems look like individual trees, but they are genetically identical parts of one tree linked by a shared root system.
evidence.quote: Pando has an estimated 47,000 stems (ramets) that appear to be individual trees but are genetically identical parts of a single tree connected by a root system

evidence.claim: That system spans 106 acres.
evidence.quote: a root system that spans 42.8 ha (106 acres).

evidence.claim: Jerry Kemperman and Burton V. Barnes identified the clone in 1976; genetic analysis published in 2008 confirmed the earlier work.
evidence.quote: The Pando tree was identified in 1976 by Jerry Kemperman and Burton V. Barnes.

evidence.claim: genetic analysis published in 2008 confirmed the earlier work.
evidence.quote: A large-scale genetic sampling and analysis was published in 2008 by Jennifer DeWoody, Karen Mock, Valerie Hipkins, and Carol Rowe. The research team's genetic study confirmed morphological analysis

evidence.claim: Its stems die individually and are replaced by new, genetically identical stems sent up from the roots.
evidence.quote: stems, which die individually and are replaced by genetically identical stems that are sent up from the tree's vast root system

evidence.claim: The age of the whole clone cannot be determined from tree rings.
evidence.quote: the overall age of an aspen clone cannot be determined from tree rings.

evidence.claim: Friends of Pando and Fishlake National Forest work together to study and protect the tree, alongside the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources.
evidence.quote: Friends of Pando and the Fishlake National Forest partner to study and protect Pando, working alongside the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources.

evidence.quote: It lies within and is the namesake of the Fishlake National Forest.
